utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, good morning. Your Honour, may I introduce a member of our team who I think has not been in court before. On my far left is Mr. Andrej Jonovic. Again, the other faces are familiar to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, thank you very much. Welcome in court. I would like to repeat your name. It's not written clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's Andrej, A-n-d-r-e-j; Jonovic, J-o-n-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jonovic, welcome in court. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed with the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Egrlic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But not until after I've reminded you, Mr. Egrlic, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. I take it that's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I think possibly overnight, you have been deprived of P228 which we were looking at yesterday. It's all part of the good order of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could have P228 back again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, we looked at points 1 to 13 yesterday. I want to ask you about point number 14, which was "Request Radio Banja Luka to broadcast one hour of programme time daily on the war events from Croatia." Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Radio Kljuc broadcast for one hour in this manner. As far as Radio Banja Luka is concerned, I know that they had already started with such programming before this date, because it was possible for us to listen to Radio Banja Luka in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Egrlic, you have been asked about these matters in this exhibit, P228, previously, and you were asked in the trial of Mr. Brdjanin. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in that particular trial, you were asked, for example, about item number 1 on this list: "Immediately form a command of the town and set up round-the-clock duty." What you told Their Honours in this trial yesterday was that that was done immediately. That's at page 69 of yesterday's transcript. "That was done immediately." You think a couple of days later. There was then quite a lot of questioning and answers from you in which you indicated that really some of this had already happened before, and then we explored what changes there had been. In the trial of Mr. Brdjanin, you were asked whether that point was implemented immediately after 29th of October, and you said: "I'm not sure if immediately, but later on, yes, indeed." And then you were asked, "Well, later on would have been 1992, wouldn't it?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be helpful if Mr. Stewart could refer us to the page number of the transcript in the Brdjanin trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I beg your pardon, of course I will do that. It's 10.625. I'm afraid I can't give the date right now, but we could easily get hold of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's usually on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour. But it isn't in this case because of where we printed it out from, so if I had it, I would give it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is 14 October 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, in that trial you said -- you were asked, "Well, later on would have been 1992, wouldn't it?" And then you said: "I found out about it in early 1992." Now, that is different, Mr. Egrlic. There's no question about that. Is the position that you really don't have at all a clear recollection of such matters now?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I don't remember the details, but it is quite possible that as far as the dates are concerned, I might not have mentioned the same dates since several years have passed since that time. But I could provide you with the periods for certain events, but as far as the exact dates are concerned, exact dates of very prominent incidents, I would find this a little more difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we take item 11, for example, on the list, in the Brdjanin trial at page 10.629, there's a very short exchange. The point was put to you as a question, number 11 was read out, and you were asked: "Do you know if that was done?" And you said: "I don't know." In this trial yesterday, I asked you whether such lists were made --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, something is coming -- all right. It's dealt with, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you whether such lists were made, and you said there were lists in shops, and yes, such lists were made. Who made them? Made by commissions from trading companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question that's asked in the Brdjanin trial is a different way of asking the question to the way Mr. Stewart asked it. And I just would like to say at this stage without foreshadowing precisely the point I'm making, if Mr. Stewart could be sure in his question to relate to the witness the entirety of his answer regarding point 11, which was not only an answer to Mr. Stewart's first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was doing although I was interrupted in the course of doing it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's begin again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we have no Brdjanin transcript available as a Bench. As soon as there's any dispute about whether parts of questions or answers are correctly stated, then the party is invited to literally quote those parts so that there can be no confusion. The Chamber is not otherwise in a position to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say first of all, there is absolutely no need for the Trial Chamber to check it because of course I would not misrepresent the position, and you have my professional assurance that will not happen. But as a matter of fact, in relation to this matter I am proposing largely simply to quote verbatim from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said to you yesterday -- I read point 11, and I said, "First of all, were such lists made?" Your answer was: "There were lists in shops --" this is in this trial. And yes, such lists were made. My question was who made them? Your answer was they were made by commissions from trading companies. Question: "Did you ever see any such list?" Answer: "No, but I do know that lists were made." Now, may I remind you that the quotation from - and Your Honour, with respect - the quotation from the Brdjanin transcript was that extremely short exchange. "Do you know if that was done?" was the question in Brdjanin. And your answer was: "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, "Do you know whether that was done or not," of course without context has no meaning whatsoever. I don't know whether it relates to item 1 to item 11 to item 14 to another document to whatever. And I think that's the issue Mr. Margetts made where you responded in a rather irritated way. That's -- if you put a question to this witness, there should be agreement between the parties what it is about in order for the Chamber to understand what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise if I betrayed any irritation, although I do accept that I was irritated because the position is this, and I would do my very best not to betray any such feelings. The position is this, Your Honour: I'm quite happy to send somebody out of court to photocopy these pages of the Brdjanin transcript, but I do like, if possible, Your Honour, not to engage in wasteful copying of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking for copying. I just say that if you say the quotation from the Brdjanin transcript was extremely short, is "Do you know if that was done?" That could relate to whatever. I think that -- yes, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the Brdjanin transcript, when it's quoted in its full, it says as follows: The question at page 10.629, line 17 is: "Number 11, 'Make lists of surplus goods as well as shortages and inform SDS Sarajevo, Mr. Ilic, about this.' Do you know if that was done?" And at line 20, the answer is: "I don't know." What I anticipated was going to be the problem with the Mr. Stewart's question in fact turned out to be precisely the problem with Mr. Stewart's question. And that is that there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to ask the witness to take his headphones off?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it would be a good idea, Your Honour, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you assist the witness in taking his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be more appropriate if the headphones were detached from the system so hat there's no translation coming through in the headphones whilst they lie on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, have you taken out the -- yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The issue with this item 11 is there's two components to it, and they were dealt with as two components yesterday by Mr. Stewart. In the Brdjanin trial, they're not dealt with in two components. They're compounded. The issues in number 11 are, one, were lists made; two, were lists provided to Mr. Ilic? The witness clearly stated yesterday in respect of lists being made that they were made; and in respect of whether they were provided to Mr. Ilic, he does not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He doesn't know Mr. Ilic, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, on the basis of this observation, would it be possible for you to deal with the matter in a way which would avoid whether you are -- the source of it is another question, but in such a way that everyone will think that questions are crystal clear and there could be no confusion whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I find it very difficult to see what more I could have done than do what I could do. When I was quoting the Brdjanin question, I said if we take item 11, for example, on the list, in the Brdjanin trial at page 10.629, there's a very short exchange. "The point was put to you as a question, number 11 was read out, and you were asked, 'Do you know if that was done?' And you said, 'I don't know.'" That was a hundred per cent verbatim accurate citation of what was in the Brdjanin trial. I was then interrupted by an objection before I had even got through quoting to the witness and putting before the Trial Chamber what was said in the exchange yesterday. Your Honour, I absolutely cannot accept the criticism of my first question which could not have been clearer. It was a verbatim hundred per cent accurate citation of the previous trial, and the objection to my question is absolutely unfounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, the way it is presented by Mr. Stewart indicates that the witness answered on the whole of the question with a clear no. He doesn't know. That would include both elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The answer in the Brdjanin trial is, "I don't know whether item 11 was implemented." The only issue we have with Mr. Stewart's question is that when he is quoting back the witness's answers from yesterday, he is only quoting the witness's answer in respect of the first component of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if the witness is confronted, Mr. Stewart, with any inconsistency, I do understand from Mr. Margetts that he considers where there was a no on all elements of the questions in Brdjanin, that in this trial yesterday he testified a partial no, that is, not knowing -- knowing about the lists and not knowing about the report to Mr. Ilic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm entitled to say this so that we know where we're going. Mr. Margetts' interjection was a comment, it was not a valid objection at all. It was used to make a comment, and I do invite the Trial Chamber not to allow the Prosecution to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather continue now, so Mr. Stewart, you may continue after the witness has been -- put his headphones on again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at point number 3, Mr. Egrlic. In the Brdjanin trial you were asked, after the completion of a short exchange of question and answer in relation to point number 2, because counsel in that case was going through the points one after the another in numerical order, that was the context. Having finished with point number 2, a short exchange at page 10.627, counsel Mr. Ackerman's question was: "Form units for the front and designate their replacements." Question: "Do you know if that was done?" Answer: "This was done when the units of the Knin Corps arrived at Laniste." Question: "And when was that?" Answer: "That was in March 1992." Question: "Five months after this document?" Answer: "At the time of this document, there were units of volunteers who went to Croatia to take part in the war there." That was the conclusion of the questioning on point number 3 in the Brdjanin case, Mr. Ackerman then went on to point number 4. Yesterday, I asked you this at page 74: "The third item - which I then quoted in exactly the same words as appear in the document and as Mr. Ackerman had done - my question, "Was that done?" as opposed to Mr. Ackerman's question, "Do you know if that was done?" Your answer: "Yes, it was." My question: "And when was that done?" Same question, very slightly differently phrased to Mr. Ackerman's question. Your answer: "It was done immediately after this decision was made, and earlier on, too, as I have said, this decision only reinforced this matter, and it continued in this manner until May." So with your extra comment in the Brdjanin case about there being units of volunteers who went to Croatia to take part in the war there, in the Brdjanin case you said it was done in March 1992; in this case, you said it was done immediately after the decision was made. Now, which, if either, of those is correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true to say that former JNA units came to the Laniste side, and it's also true to say that units were formed of the local population. This started in August and continued up until May. So how should I put it? There were two types of units that were formed; a unit formed by the population from Kljuc and from part of the units that came to Laniste. I don't know which places the members of those units were from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Point number 4, Mr. Egrlic -- I'm not going to go through every Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond point, so nobody need, not unless the Trial Chamber directs me to cover all that ground. But number 4, in the Brdjanin case, quite a short exchange. Immediately after the conclusion of the questions and answers I've just quoted on point number 3, question from Mr. Ackerman, number 4: "All men under the age of 40 to be reassigned from civilian protection to the Territorial Defence and the Territorial Defence to be resubordinated to the corps as wartime units." "Did that happen?" Answer: "I don't know about that, because I didn't see any evidence or documents about this." And then counsel went on to point 5. Yesterday, at page 75, I quoted item 4 in exactly the same terms as translated in the document in front of us, P228. And I asked: "Did that happen?" Which was in fact precisely the same question that Mr. Ackerman had asked you. And your answer was: "Yes, it did." And I asked you: "You know that, do you?" You said: "I do." I asked you, "How do you know it?" You answered: "Well, I know that because in the Secretariat for National Defence there was a clerk who was still working there. He was a Bosniak, and he told me that as far as cards, et cetera, were concerned, this should be done, and these units for fighting in the battlefield in Croatia should be formed." My question was, "And when did you first come to know about that?" And your answer was: "I came to know about that sometime in November 1991." Now, Mr. Egrlic, those are different. I can make that assertion without any fear of serious contradiction. Why, on the basis of your solemn declaration in the Brdjanin case, why didn't you tell the Court in the Brdjanin case what you told this Trial Chamber yesterday? Why did you tell the Brdjanin trial that you didn't know about this point?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were talking in that context about whether I had seen any documents referring to this. On the basis of that, I said I didn't have this information. Yesterday, I said that I hadn't seen any documents, but that I had heard about it, as I explained. And this did happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's an absolutely misleading and untrue answer, I put to you, Mr. Egrlic. You were asked the question in the Brdjanin case in exactly the simplest terms in which you were asked it yesterday, and it was your answer "I don't know about that," and your explanation of why you didn't know about it was then because you hadn't seen any evidence or documents about this. Let me make it clear, Mr. Egrlic, you did not say that you knew something but not from documents, you simply said in the Brdjanin case you didn't know. And yesterday, you came out with some stuff that you say you did know. Which is it, Mr. Egrlic? Did you know about this in 1991 or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm minded that you do not have the transcript before you of the Brdjanin trial, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have at this moment the relevant page in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the last question, and that was where it was left because you hadn't yet answered it, was did you know about this in 1991 or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew -- I did know, but I had no documents. It was on the basis of what this gentleman who worked in the secretariat told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you understand? Let's get it clear, Mr. Egrlic, when you're asked in the course of this trial, or any other trial for that matter, when you're asked whether you know something, you understand that question in some qualified way, do you, that you can only say yes if you've seen some documents or seen some hard evidence? Is that your understanding of the question "Do you know something"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can find things out on the basis of documents or on the basis of conversations. In the previous trial, the way the question was put to me, the way I understood it and answered it, was that you can say on the basis of documents that you know something. I had no documents. All I had was the statement of the person who told me, and this is not in dispute. People were recruited, and they did go off to the battlefield. Every citizen of Kljuc knows this. I don't think anything will change if you try to convince me I said one thing then and something else today. Nothing will change. People did go away. They went to war. They came back, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just if I may, with respect, make it clear to the Trial Chamber now, I'm not proposing, because I don't consider it's necessary, in fairness to the witness or anybody else, to go through point by point identifying differences between what was said in the Brdjanin trial and differences in this trial because I've explored one or two of them. Your Honour has seen the outcome of that recent exchange. It becomes, eventually, a matter of comment and argument to place what this witness said in one trial alongside what he said in the other trial, and I suggest that it would be unnecessarily time consuming and not necessary, in fairness, for me to go through these points one by one to highlight those differences and obtain the witness's comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we have heard what he said. We'll assess the meaning of the issues you just raised. I mean, it's entirely up to you how to use your time for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder perhaps if the witness should take his headphones off just briefly for the next...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I undertake not to quote back to you too irresponsibly Your Honour's comment that it's entirely up to me how I use my time for cross-examination. But I'm grateful for that, Your Honour. What I had mind was that -- I don't want it to be suggested later that it was not fair to this witness and it's not fair for me later to draw attention in submissions to discrepancies between the evidence in the Brdjanin case, the evidence in this case on the basis I didn't go through it point by point with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with that, but on the other hand you seem to suggest or to speculate on what the result is of dealing with the two examples out of the list, suggesting that you showed in all respects the contradictions between them. I also noted that sometimes the language of the witness is a bit inconsistent. For example, when you asked him yesterday a question about 11, Did it happen? He said yes. And then you said, Do you know? And then he started explaining an explanation which clearly indicates that his previous answer was meant in a different way as literally said because the question was "Did that happen" means were these units formed? Whereas he later says in his explanation, he says "I heard from someone that it should be done." So therefore, it is a -- certainly you have pointed at differences in his testimony in the Brdjanin case and in this case, but I would say there's more to be said about -- at least, whether there's anything to be said about it is a different matter, but it could raise -- the whole analysis of his testimony in the Brdjanin case and the testimony he gave yesterday here might give rise to more questions than only the ones you've put to him even in respect of these two items on the list. So that's what I intended to say when I said up to you, I would say, whether to spend more time on this issue or on other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think what I'll do, Your Honour, in the circumstances, then, is I will move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought it was fair for at least -- just speaking as one of the Judges, it's fair to make clear that what you more or less suggested or expected as what would be the understanding of the Chamber of the testimony given this morning in the confrontation between the two, that it was perhaps even more complex than you suggested, not to say that you suggested it was an easy matter, but that there were other things to be noted. I just wanted to make it clear to you so that you'd be better able to decide whether to further explore this matter or to go to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, what I was going to suggest, Your Honour, is I would go to another topic, which although I shan't be an enormously long time with the witness, I think the next topic will take us to the break. And then I'm expecting to finish between the first and the second break today with this witness, so over the first break I will consider whether to pursue these particular points. That seems to be the more efficient way of dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. If Your Honour would give me a moment. Since I'm switching topics I therefore need to switch notes as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, it's linked to the document that we've just been looking at, but you, in your evidence on Tuesday this week, you were asked about the reference in the document to a meeting of all municipal presidents on the 26th of October 1991 in Banja Luka chaired by Dr. Karadzic. And you were asked, this is at page 39: "Did you discuss with Mr. Banjac whether or not he attended this meeting?" And your answer was: "No, I didn't, but I knew that he was in contact with him since he would travel to Banja Luka." Can we take it, Mr. Egrlic, that since you didn't discuss with Mr. Banjac whether or not he attended this meeting, you never had any sort of discussion with Mr. Banjac about any of the content of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any sort of discussion with him about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any discussion with anybody else about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about the document -- which at the moment I've mislaid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. That I've now retrieved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked whether you personally came to a conclusion as to whether or not Mr. Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic, as he is, knew of these 14 steps set out in the document. And your answer was: "It says on the document that it was drafted in agreement with Mr. Karadzic, so it is beyond any dispute that he knew." Maybe a small point, Mr. Egrlic: Do you agree it doesn't actually say on the document that it was drafted in agreement with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document before me, so I can't say it with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not the document at your left elbow, Mr. Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, it might not be clear to the witness that this document is about the decisions of 1991 because it does not appear in the heading of it. I think there's some confusion. I think it's the right document, yes. Perhaps you better introduce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought I had made it clear by referring to the link, but apparently not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, the document that you have on the table in front of you is the same one that we were looking at five, ten minutes ago, and it's the same one that I wish you to be looking at now. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is in English, and I don't understand what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you shouldn't be given a document in English. Is the one in front of you -- you're holding in your hand now, is that in English or in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in B/C/S now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apology if I caused any misunderstanding there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- we'll go back to the question then. Your answer on Tuesday was, "It says on the document that it was drafted in agreement with Mr. Karadzic, so it is beyond any dispute that he knew." So just on the first bit of that answer you gave, just to try and be clear, do you agree, it doesn't, in fact, say on the document that it was drafted in agreement with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document says "chaired by Dr. Karadzic" or "under the leadership of Dr. Karadzic."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- do you agree, Mr. Egrlic, that it does not say that it was drafted in agreement with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the document, no, it doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Egrlic, is the position that you know no more about this question of how the points -- how this document came to be drafted, who was involved in the drafting, you know no more than can be gathered from the words of the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't attend that session, so I can't say who was there. It's only on the basis of this document. And on the basis of the fact that I know that Mr. Banjac and Mr. Kondic went and contacted Banja Luka. This is beyond dispute. And it was quite normal that they should go and contact somebody there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then an answer that you gave just a very few lines later on, on page 43 of Tuesday's transcript in this case, was you said, "I can see from the document that the leadership of the party drafted this order and forwarded it to the lower levels down to the municipal committees or boards." So, Mr. Egrlic, again, what you were talking about there was only what you were able to gather from the written terms of the document in front of you. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be quite normal to expect if this was done under the leadership of Dr. Karadzic, or rather that the meeting was chaired by Dr. Karadzic, that the top party leadership should be aware of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's this, Mr. Egrlic, that I'm putting to you: Apart from the fact that you knew, you have told the Trial Chamber, you knew that Mr. Banjac, you say, had been to Banja Luka, and you can see this document, and you know who Dr. Karadzic was, you have no personal knowledge beyond that on the basis of which you can offer the Trial Chamber any more information about this document.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your evidence, then, immediately after the answer I quoted to you a moment ago, you said, "The leader of the SDS at that time was Mr. Karadzic, and in his inner circle was Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Koljevic, and so on and so forth." That was your precise answer. First of all, when you said "and so on and so forth," did you have in mind some other people in addition to Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who are those other people?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a wide circle of people who were close to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Egrlic, may I just remind you, in fairness, that your answer was specifically concerned with the inner circle. That was your phrase, in fact; it came from you, the phrase. It wasn't in the question. The question that you were asked by Mr. Margetts was, "Who did you think constituted the leadership in Sarajevo?" You referred to Mr. Karadzic as the leader. You then produced the phrase "inner circle." You said, "In his inner circle was Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Mr. Koljevic and so on." So did you have in mind there were other people then in addition to those three in Mr. Karadzic's inner circle?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I thought there were other people who belonged there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were they as you understood it at the time in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the inner circle, there was Brdjanin. Those were the best-known people as far as I was concerned. I can't recall the names of the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- and let's try and cast your mind back to October, November 1991 as best we can, Mr. Egrlic. What was your knowledge of Mr. Karadzic's inner circle based upon?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the fact that every session -- almost every session was broadcast on the public media, it was reported in the press, and it was no secret. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Every session of what?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sessions of the assembly, the party sessions, and so on. You could read about all that in the newspapers. You could read who was there, who the people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the position, Mr. Egrlic, is that you -- your knowledge on the basis of which you express views about the inner circle was the same knowledge that any individual living where you lived with access to newspapers and television would have had?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had no more knowledge of the inner circle membership or any other aspect of Mr. Karadzic's inner circle than any such citizen living where you lived with access to newspapers and television.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, what I know comes from the public media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's the other part, then, Mr. Egrlic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other part refers to what I heard from Mr. Banjac when he told me who he had met with, and I thought this was quite normal, that he would meet those people. I didn't see anything unusual in this. I simply knew that these were the leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party, the representatives in the then organs of government, and I knew which people constituted the narrow circle of leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did Mr. Banjac tell you he had met?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually he would meet Mr. Brdjanin in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you of meeting any of the other people that you mentioned in relation to Mr. Karadzic's inner circle?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He mentioned Mr. Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic, he mentioned Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about -- Mr. Banjac is dead now. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he die?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, he died about one year ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about your -- well, you gave evidence about your daily meetings with Mr. Banjac in 1991. And you told this Trial Chamber - this is at page 55 of Tuesday's transcript - that you noticed towards the end of 1991 and beginning of 1992 there were some very important issues in the territory of the municipality and that he wasn't able to deal with them on his own until he had consulted with the higher authorities. Can you give a specific example of such an important issue that he was not able to deal with on his own?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do have an example. When it was necessary to change the insignia on the uniforms, he persuaded us that he couldn't do this on his own. So he arranged for a meeting in Banja Luka. I have already mentioned this, and this is a specific example I can provide you with. In that case, he wasn't able to resolve the issue at the municipal level alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to pursue that particular point, Mr. Egrlic, for the simple reason that you've already given quite a lot of evidence on that particular specific topic. Do you have any other example that you can give this Trial Chamber of such an issue on which Mr. Banjac wasn't able to deal with the matter on his own?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any other particular examples apart from the one that I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about a conversation that you'd had with Mr. Banjac outside a restaurant in Kljuc, and he had talked about an exodus. This was at page 57 of Wednesday's transcript this week. He said, "People would have to be moved from this territory. There would have to be an exodus of people from this territory." You asked him, "What kind of exodus, how do you mean moving people? How can that be carried out?" And he said, "From some territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbs had to leave; from others, Bosniaks and Croats had to leave so that their respective minority percentages would not be more than 5 or 6 per cent." "I told him this was plain crazy. I couldn't understand anybody could have conceived that in their head and this was totally undo-able. And this was how our conversation in front of the restaurant ended. Then we entered the restaurant itself." Well, first of all, there was clearly a very strong difference of view between your view and what Mr. Banjac had been talking about. Was the position, though, that as between you and Mr. Banjac, relations continued to be good on a personal level?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said a few lines after that answer, you said, "It seemed to me that he personally did not share that view, but that he would be willing to implement what had been outlined by the policy." Now, were there other SDS representatives or leaders in Kljuc with whom Mr. Banjac might have disagreed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I think that he agreed with everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the first question is -- all right, perhaps I better put it a different way. He wasn't the only active person in the local leadership of the SDS in Kljuc, was he?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He wasn't the only person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was the one that you spoke to the most and the most often, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said Mr. Banjac always consulted with the higher bodies for all important decisions. You've mentioned the insignia point. But does it follow from the fact that a few minutes ago you weren't able to point to any other examples, specific example, of something that Mr. Banjac was not able to deal with on his own, that you're also unable to point to any other example where Mr. Banjac consulted with higher bodies?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did consult with them over the phone, and I'm quite convinced that he didn't take decisions on his own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what I'm asking you, Mr. Egrlic, is - I'll give you another opportunity, in effect - can you -- leave aside the insignia point, you've given evidence about that and visit to Banja Luka, and so on. Can you give this Trial Chamber any other specific example of an issue on which Mr. Banjac consulted higher bodies?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the Municipality of Kljuc joining the Autonomous Region of Krajina is concerned, this certainly wasn't the idea of the SDS leadership in Kljuc. It was the idea of the leadership in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, can you tell the Trial Chamber any specific issue on which you know that Mr. Banjac consulted higher bodies?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already given you an example. Is it necessary to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean the insignia example?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, there seems to be some misunderstanding. That's the following: You mentioned topics on which you think the -- Mr. Banjac in Kljuc would follow policy set out by higher levels rather than doing what he himself would have done. Mr. Stewart is asking you not whether there are any topics where you think that he did follow what higher up levels would have deemed appropriate but whether you have some knowledge of Mr. Banjac consulting in whatever way - by telephone, by writing, by going there - on those topics. So you identified the topics, and the second part of the question, implied second part of the question is can you tell us what you know about any such consultations on those topics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was with him at a meeting in Banja Luka that concerned the change of insignia. And as far as Kljuc joining the autonomous region is concerned, some documents arrived from Banja Luka, the statute of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka arrived, and this is clear proof that it came from a higher level. That document was present in the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, this is probably going to be the last opportunity I will offer you on this point. The -- may I simply, with respect and subject to the direction of the Trial Chamber, remind you that the question of evidence and clear proof, et cetera, et cetera, that's what this Trial Chamber is here to do, to evaluate everything and reach such conclusions. You are a witness, Mr. Egrlic. You are invited to tell the Trial Chamber what you know. So the opportunity I'm offering you is to tell the Trial Chamber what, if anything, you know about consultation by Mr. Banjac with higher bodies on important decisions, leaving aside those insignia, please.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have repeated this a number of times now. Perhaps we don't understand each other sufficiently well. But I said that Mr. Banjac often went to Banja Luka and held discussions there. And as far as the insignia are concerned, I said that we went there, and I said that with regard to the Autonomous Region of Krajina, documents arrived from Banja Luka, and according to these documents, the Municipality of Kljuc was supposed to be annexed. These, in my opinion, are very concrete examples. This is concrete proof, and I have no other examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just ask an additional question. Mr. Egrlic, you're asked about consultations, and you told us that since the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was sent to Kljuc, that this really demonstrates how things came from a higher level. I'm asking you the following: Just imagine for argument's sake that it would have been the sincere wish of people in Kljuc to join that autonomous region - I know that that's not what you testified, but let's just assume that - would you not need the statute of the autonomous region under these circumstances as well? So it should then be sent to you? Do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it would be necessary to have the statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you refer to sending and receiving the statute of the autonomous region, and in your later answer you said documents arrived, which I do understand to be reference to the previous answer about the statute being received from Banja Luka in Kljuc, that is not an answer to consultations. Of course, it could be part of consultations. Sending documents may well be a part of consultations, but what Mr. Stewart specifically asked you and what the Chamber very much would like to have an answer to is do you know any other circumstance, for example, if Mr. Banjac would have called to Banja Luka and would have said, well, I don't know what you want from me, but if you want me to do this or this, then at least send me some documents so I know what your wish is and what I should follow. These are concrete facts about consultations. Could you provide us with any concrete facts about how and when and on what subject Mr. Banjac consulted, so apart from the insignia, consulted the higher up levels for instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other concrete examples apart from the ones that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the frequency between, well, let's say Banja Luka and Kljuc as far as telephone communications are concerned between Mr. Banjac and higher up levels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, even before, Banja Luka was a regional centre for the surrounding municipalities, and one would go to Banja Luka every week at least once a week, so contact was maintained in this way. As to how often telephone contact was made, I couldn't say. But people did go to Banja Luka very often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you any specific knowledge on what they did and, if there was any discussion, what they discussed when they were in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you were asked specifically when higher levels of the SDS party visited Kljuc -- this is page 59 of Wednesday's transcript, 28th of July. You said, "Some did. Mr. Nikola Koljevic, who was a member of the Presidency. There was one such meeting." I believe it's clear from that phrase in the English "a member of the Presidency" that the word must have been "Presidency" rather than "president" because otherwise the answer would make no sense. But what do you mean by "the Presidency"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the Presidency of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. And it is in that capacity that he came to Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time are we talking about? What date?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1991, perhaps in the first half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you said that Mr. Karadzic came a lot later, that you can't remember when. You saw Mr. Karadzic, did you, in Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw him on one occasion when the party was being founded, but I didn't see the arrival because I didn't attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have -- even if you didn't see him yourself or attend meetings, would you have always known whether Mr. Karadzic had visited Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this case, yes, because it was a public meeting. And there were no secrets. Anyone who wanted to see him could see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what I mean, Mr. Egrlic, and was inviting you to confirm, Kljuc is not New York. Can we take it that if somebody like Mr. Karadzic, who was certainly a prominent figure, visited Kljuc at that time, most of the people in Kljuc, and certainly you, would know that that had happened. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did Mr. Karadzic visit Kljuc in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only aware of him visiting Kljuc on that one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber how often he visited Kljuc in the first four months of 1992, January to April?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about him visiting Kljuc then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say how often Mr. Koljevic visited Kljuc in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended one such official meeting, and I heard that he came on one other occasion afterwards in the settlement of Ribnik. But on that occasion, he didn't go to the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you say how often Mr. Koljevic visited Kljuc in the first four months of 1992, January to April?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But does the same apply to Mr. Koljevic, that if he visited Kljuc, you would have come to know about it, Mr. Egrlic? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if it was an official visit, I would certainly have known about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just that in a statement that you gave, and it's a very short passage, this, I'm not trying to keep back the statement from you in any way, Mr. Egrlic, the statement you gave to representatives of this Tribunal on the 22nd of May 1997, you said: "On many occasions during 1991, Mr. Karadzic and Nikola Koljevic visited Kljuc." It now seems that "many occasions" actually is clearly an exaggeration. Do you accept that now?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a single member of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that if someone comes to a place twice or even just once officially, I think that this means that the person has visited the place frequently. In my opinion, this means that the person visited the place frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, this point doesn't need any --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I entirely agree, Your Honour. And we are a few minutes over the normal run, but this might be a convenient point for Your Honour to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before the break, Your Honour, I just wanted to foreshadow an issue, that the following witness after this one is one that we have protective measures for and so there may need to be some break when we do that. In addition, Your Honour, I would request, if possible with the Court, if we could complete that witness today because he's been Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond here all week, lost a lot of work and we're not going to sit again until the end of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need for him? Because he was scheduled for four hours, so I had in mind as a matter of fact that it would be -- it doesn't make any sense. He has to come back anyhow for cross-examination unless -- but I do know that it might cause great difficulties to even continue this afternoon because of the absence of Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I wanted to raise the possibility perhaps going half an hour longer, depending on how far we get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We think maybe two hours for his direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, how much time would you still need for the further -- perhaps I'll first ask the witness to leave the courtroom. We'll have a break for 25 minutes, Mr. Egrlic. We would like to see you back after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that I probably need no more than about 10 minutes for -- I expect, to helpfully answer Your Honour's question, 10 minutes plus anything that I decide I might need to go into in relation to those 14 points, the matter I was going to consider over the break. If I do have to go through those points, then to some extent it's in the witness's hands and how he answers them, that could add on 20 minutes or half an hour easily. But it won't be more than that, Your Honour. So I should comfortably finish, on any footing, within 45 minutes, and hopefully within 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see where we come, because there's no way -- perhaps five minutes but not an hour. You understand that just prior to the recess that schedules have been prepared. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 11.00. Let's try, and I'm also addressing the Chamber itself, to start in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I addressed ourselves to be here at 5 minutes to 11.00. The explanation is that still a decision is expected from us, and that kept us busy. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour will be pleased anyway to know that, having considered the matter over the break, I don't propose to go through those further 14 points. But what I would wish to do, Your Honour, is to tender that passage, that section of the transcript from the Brdjanin case. With the apology, Your Honour, that over the break we've only been able to get the pages off the internet which are not in quite as neat form as the official transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the -- I think the questioning on the document starts on page 10.625, the transcript of the 14th of October. And it relates to what was then E22 -- it even starts already a bit earlier. Let me just see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think Your Honour is absolutely right, with respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then we have 625, 10.626 is an empty page. Then it would be 627, 628, 629, 630, and I think it ends -- 14 is on page 630, and then it goes a bit further in the answer "I thought that when I said most of them, I was referring to the most important of these items." Would that be sufficient or would you need 631 as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour has, I think, exactly the right pages. We felt that 10.631 should probably be included just for completeness so it can be seen how the passage finishes. But otherwise, starting -- we've started with -- well, it has a little bit of 10.624 because that's on the same page, but 10.625, as Your Honour identified it, going through to 631, that covers it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That, Mr. Registrar, would have what number? I would rather make it as an exhibit because there's no 92 bis (d) application, so Mr. Margetts, unless you would disagree, the Chamber is inclined to allow this part of the transcript just as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we agree to that part of the transcript being allowed. I'm just looking through the re-examination by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you do that perhaps -- we'll take a final decision on it. If there would be any suggestions in that respect, we'll hear from you soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I couldn't possibly object to any linked passages from the re-examination transcript going in. Your Honour, shall I hand those in? Those are the internet printouts, but frankly, they are perfectly good enough for working purposes. What would Your Honour like me to do about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, are dates and numbers on it, and the case? Everything's on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, they are. They're in a only thinly coded form. Yes, 02/10/14, it's there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I asked Mr. Registrar to provide us with a number, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number will be D25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D25 for some pages of transcript from the Brdjanin. And there could be additions to that. Yes. There are dates on it, but these are the dates when you printed it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think -- Your Honour I think the date appears --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think the date appears from the numbering at the bottom and at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that it's a code 02 is the year, 10 is the month, and 14 is the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's that strange backwards way of doing it, Your Honour, once we get used to doing it. That's when I meant when I said thinly coded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's finally deal with that. Even if necessary, we'll not go through the exhibits anyhow before the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can sort it out then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they're there and whether anything will be added, we'll see that at a later stage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, that's very helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you went, didn't you -- in the summer of 1991, presidents of the executive boards were invited to a meeting with what I think you described as the economic association in Banja Luka. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went accompanied with -- or rather, you met Mirzet Karabeg before you went into that meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We met in Banja Luka because he, too, came to attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Egrlic, I'm sorry, I should have made that clear. I said you didn't meet in Banja Luka. So you met in Banja Luka, as you say, but you met before the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the meeting in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went into the meeting together?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at some point, you came to the conclusion you were just in the wrong meeting and you left within a very short time. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't stay and listen to any speeches?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Yes, that's to say neither of you stayed and listened to speeches; neither you nor Mr. Karabeg.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, it's right, is it, of course you see Mr. Krajisnik in this courtroom, but you have never met Mr. Krajisnik in your life, have you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in 1991, 1992, and into 1993, you had -- is it correct you'd never seen Mr. Krajisnik in your life at that point in person, as opposed to on television?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik never came to Kljuc. In 1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, he never once came to Kljuc, did he?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to make it complete, you're not aware of him ever coming to Kljuc before 1990, are you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, is there any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two very short matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Mr. Margetts:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you were just referred to a meeting which you attended in Banja Luka. How did you come to attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received an invitation as the president of the executive board to attend the meeting, and I went as did Mr. Mirzet Karabeg from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the meeting, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I observed that colleagues from neighbouring municipalities were absent, those who were Bosniaks. We expected this to be a broad-based, mixed meeting of all representatives of municipalities regardless of their nationality or ethnicity, and we thought that people we knew from neighbouring municipalities such as Prijedor would be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was in 1991, maybe in the first half of that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there only Serbs present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to conclude, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to identify any of the individuals at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On arrival at the meeting, Mr. Mirzet Karabeg and I sat down, and not far from where we were sitting we saw Mr. Brdjanin with some other people sitting there. He was three or four seats away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brdjanin say anything?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was having a vehement discussion with the people around him and I heard him say, "We Serbs would achieve a lot if we were to achieve our political goal of getting Republika Srpska. That would mean a lot to us."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything in addition to that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall every detail, but we both heard that. And seeing that we were out of place at that meeting, we got up and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible that after you left the meeting, Mr. Karabeg returned to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not possible because he went off in the direction of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your conclusion as to whether or not you should have received the invitation to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the conclusion was that we were not welcome there because there was no one else there from the other municipalities and because we heard this statement that Mr. Brdjanin made, and we saw that there would be a discussion on political topics rather than economic ones, which was what the invitation said, and we were not authorised to speak about political issues. Therefore, we decided that we were out of place there and we left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the invitation to the Court.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the details, but like every invitation, it contained the agenda and the preamble, and it said "Serbian Autonomous Province of Bosnian Krajina," and I don't recall who signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do recall, as you just said, that it referred to economic issues; yet, in fact, the meeting dealt with political issues.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, you were asked a number of questions in respect of matters that Mr. Banjac could or could not deal with on his own. I would just like to ask you some very brief questions on that issue. You had a very close relationship with Mr. Banjac, and you did come to know the type of issues that he could deal with on his own and the issues he did not have much influence over. I'm just going to name a few issues and ask you to tell me whether or not he could deal with these matters on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. This is dangerously into a leading area. I asked this witness and gave him several opportunities, and Your Honour also, with questions, gave the witness the fairest opportunity to answer this question. If there is a genuine re-examination question, that's another matter, but re-examination cannot properly be used to put leading questions to try to extract answers when the witness has answered non-leading questions already in relation to that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts -- could you please take your earphones off for a second. Mr. Margetts, the witness has clearly answered questions about consultations and factual knowledge on how Mr. Banjac would have acted on instructions, et cetera. That did not result in a lot of information. Now you're referring to his general good relationship with him. And I take it that you're going to feed him some bits and pieces of where you would expect that -- this is about facts and not about saying wouldn't you think that on the basis of your good relationship that on this and this issue that he might not have been in a position to deal with the matter himself and how did you get that impression? If there are specific fields you think there's a good reason to ask him such questions because you have an idea that he would know some facts, then please tell us now in advance so that we know why we would allow you to put such questions to the witness against the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll be guided by the Court on this matter. The issue we have here is that we have a witness who is in a very unique position to assist the Court in that he had a long-standing personal relationship with a leading SDS figure, and he had a long-standing professional relationship, both in politics and prior to that outside politics. Not only that, we have a witness who was one of the leading figures in the municipality --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- as the president of the executive committee and would have been intimately involved, as he has related in his evidence, in relation to each and every issue that the municipal assembly itself had or did not have authority over. Accordingly, this is a witness who the Prosecution submits is in a position, a unique position, to assist the Court on ascertaining the nature of the jurisdictional powers of municipal, regional, and republic-level party organs, and specifically because of his relationship with SDS figures in Kljuc, which was unique with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, may I stop you. I see that you find Mr. Egrlic a unique witness. But apart from all the things you said, this is also the witness who until now on questions "What were the specific fields where Mr. Banjac would have received instructions or been guided by," he said "I do not know any others." Then we asked questions about what he knew about. So therefore, his unique position did not materialise yet in answers of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only reason for the proposed Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond re-examination - I'll be guided by the Court's recollection of the nature of the questions in the cross-examination - is that it appeared to the Prosecution that in many of the questions, the witness was not entirely clear specifically what was being referred to and was attempting to the best of his ability to respond to the questions. The issue of confusion appeared to be arising, in the Prosecution's submission, because there was a reference to visits to Banja Luka, visits to Sarajevo. Did he meet with leading figures? Did he know that Banjac met with these figures? And he appeared to be merely basing his answers in respect of this rather crucial and important issue on whether or not he had actually obtained knowledge of meetings and the substance of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, but now you're entering in the area of facts again. I think the objection by Mr. Stewart was that where the witness until now answered on all questions "I've got no further details on consultations, I've no further details on areas in which guidance was received," that you would suggest a few areas where he would have received, or at least you would like to verify that, where he couldn't come up with it even after three, four, five questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just say this: This is something that Your Honour's in the position to assess, whether or not these questions and the answers provided are of value to you. And ultimately, it's a question of weight that may be given to any answers, taking into account the nature of the cross-examination and the natures of the answers to that and the answers to the questions that I intend to pose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you then quite clearly: If you would like to put areas to him, what would you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I just have three areas: The first area is Mobilisation, the second area is the joinder of the autonomous region, and the third area is ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will not allow you to put any additional questions in this respect, Mr. Margetts. Is there any other -- you said you had two very brief issues. The first one you dealt with, the second one was the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that's all the questions we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a few minor questions I would like to put to you in order to clarify some of your testimony. My first question is one that has to do with an answer you gave to Defence counsel's questions. Defence counsel asked you whether Bosniaks in Croatia had been mobilised, and if so, did they take part in military operations. Your answer was that it was quite possible that this had been done. And you were then asked whether it was something that was possible or whether something that you were aware of. You said that it was just a possibility. So a possibility, this is just a hypothesis. Have I understood you correctly? What made you draw the conclusion that this was a possibility?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that because from the territory of the Municipality of Kljuc, quite a lot of Bosniaks worked in the Republic of Croatia. They had been working there for a number of years. Some of them had even obtained pensions there. It is possible that they became citizens of the Republic of Croatia in this way, and as a result, the authorities in Croatia may have mobilised them. And this is perhaps how they took part in the war. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] They were mobilised by force?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I'm just talking about this in a speculative manner because I'm not aware of any concrete example. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] If we ask you the same question about the Bosniaks in Bosnia, do you completely exclude the hypothesis that they took part in the action at the side of the Serbs? Would your conclusions be the same? Would you say that the same possibility existed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now move on to another question. You said that in your opinion, the war in Croatia was an illegitimate war. And for this reason -- you said it was the reason for which the Bosniaks failed to respond to the mobilisation call-up. Is this your personal opinion? Is this the opinion of a given party? Or is this the position of what one might call the Bosniak community?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the SDA's position. The Bosniaks shouldn't have been fighting in Croatia since the SDA believed that the different way in which the republics were organised within the former Yugoslavia, they were of the opinion that the differences could be solved through agreement and not by getting involved in a war. And they thought that it wasn't necessary for the Bosniaks to take part in that war. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So in a certain sense, you were following the orders of a party.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Did this party have any presence in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Don't you find that the position taken by the party with regard to its adherence in Bosnia might not have the same position with regard to the follows in Croatia? Or are you saying that the same directives were issued by the party in Bosnia and in Croatia with regard to the follows of the same party, namely, the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to answer that. I know that as far as the party's position is concerned, it related to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As to whether these directives should have been implemented in the territory of another state, I'm not aware of that. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Who did you receive orders or directives from?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were directives issued from the Presidency of the party, the president of the party, the late Alija Izetbegovic made this publicly known over the television. And he encouraged the Bosniaks not to take part in that war and he provided certain reasons which were accepted by the Bosniaks, and they did not respond to the call-up. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And it is because of this announcement that you took a certain position according to which the war in Croatia was illegitimate; and for this reason, you believed that you should not respond to the mobilisation call-up?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. One could say that it was because of the announcement because it wasn't just anyone who made the announcement but it was the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina who made it. And on the other hand, in the Municipality of Kljuc, our opinion was identical to the opinion according to which our citizens shouldn't go to war in Croatia and die for the interests of others that we were not aware of.
