At the time, we didn't even know what the objectives were. And at no time could one have said that it was justified to send people to die there. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] What was the position of the Croats in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of their positions, positions of the Croats in Bosnia. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You didn't have any contact, you weren't aware of any contact between the parties, between the SDA and other parties with regard to the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally wasn't aware of this. There was a small number of Croats living in Kljuc, about 700 of them, as far as I can remember. And I know that they did not organise themselves in a political way and there were no discussions about that subject. I am also aware of the fact that they didn't take part in the war in Croatia. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But there was a Croatian party in Bosnia, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But you are saying that the individuals living in your community, in your village, weren't under that party, none of them were under that party?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they had not organised themselves. As to whether they were followers or adherents of that party, that's quite possible. But there was no HDZ party in Kljuc. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. I will now move on to another subject. You said that Mr. Banjac did not personally agree with the orders that he received. That's your personal impression, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And what led you to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I came to that conclusion because Mr. Banjac was a colleague of mine. He had been a colleague of mine for about ten years. And I think that I knew him. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but did he tell you, for example, that he was obliged to act in a certain way, that he had been threatened; did he say that he was not free to act as he saw fit?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I showed the telex we have discussed, then he said that the person who had issued that order was crazy. He said Brdjo is crazy, so I drew the conclusion that he did not believe that these were sound decisions. And I drew the conclusion that he did not support these ideas, that he didn't accept them. And later, on a number of occasions in the course of conversations, I noticed that there were certain things that he would not have implemented but pressure was exerted on him in the environment he was living on. This pressure came from higher levels. And when I mentioned his opinion of having people moved out of the territory, I also realised that this was not something that he wished. Sometimes you can notice these things even if a person doesn't state them explicitly. It was possible to see that this was not his wish but that he found himself in such circumstances and there was no way out for him. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] In an answer that you provided, you stated that he was probably following orders from above. If I have understood you correctly, this had to do with displacing persons. Is that, in fact, your testimony? Is that, in fact, your position?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Do you know who he was referring to? Do you know who the "hierarchy" was?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly, but there were a number of levels; the regional level and the central part of the party. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But this is an assumption you are making. You don't really have an answer; you have no information about the subject.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now move on to another subject. It has to do with you being wounded. If I have understood you correctly, you were wounded in the foot by a bullet. And you then got into a car, you were stopped at a checkpoint, and that is where you were detained. If I have understood this correctly, this was not the only wound inflicted on you. You were also wounded in other parts of your body. Have I understood your testimony correctly or not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have understood my testimony correctly to a certain extent. I was wounded in one foot. This was a gunshot wound. And as to the other wounds, after I'd been taken to the MUP, the police station, as a result of the beatings, I was wounded. And I still have the scars on my body and on my face to this very day. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] When you were taken to the police station, were you questioned? Were you accused of having done anything?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was only beaten. They then took me to the hospital in Kljuc as I was covered in blood. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. And were your wounds treated in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My wounds -- the wound to my foot was bandaged, but apart from the treatment, I was beaten again because there were Serbian troops at the entrance to the hospital and in the hospital. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Were you under surveillance in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was guarded by Serbian troops. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] How much time did you spend in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about an hour. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] So the wound was just a superficial wound, it was a slight wound?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an entry and exit wound through the foot. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But there was no hemorrhaging?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could there not be any hemorrhaging if a bullet passes through someone's foot and through someone's bone? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] But the bleeding stopped before you left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stopped after the wound had been bandaged. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. And once you had left, were you questioned again at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't discharged from the hospital but I was escorted by the Serbian police to the MUP, to the police station. I wasn't questioned there, but -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Questioned about what exactly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't questioned on that day. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Were you interrogated on subsequent dates; and if so, about what? What were you accused of?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, when they took me to the Stara Gradiska prison, after a few days they interrogated me about the Territorial Defence, about weapons possessed, et cetera. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And at the time of your arrest, did you have your pistol on you? Was it a pistol or a revolver?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have anything on me. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. But one suspects that -- one suspected that you had been wounded by a bullet.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that I had been wounded. But the pistol remained at the site where I had been wounded. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Very well. I will move on to my last question now. It has to do with the mass graves. The President of the Chamber asked you whether there were the bodies of children and women in these graves as well, and your answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Is this information that you obtained yourself because you were present at the site or is this hearsay information?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there when the mass graves were being exhumed. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Who identified the bodies?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were professional teams there that usually identify such bodies. And the families of those who had been missing until then also identified some of the bodies on the basis of the clothing that they had or on the basis of the items that they had. Some of them even had papers on them. They had their identity cards or social security card or something like that. So the vast majority of the victims were identified. Some are still listed as not having been identified, but they're now using the latest methods to identify them since the blood of their parents has been taken and they're now waiting to analyse these samples. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Did you follow the entire process of identifying these bodies? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And my very last question now: Were you quite convinced that all the bodies were the bodies of Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm quite convinced of this, and there are documents to support this. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, since I have no further questions to you, I would like to thank you -- unless there's any -- yes. On the other hand, I'd like to ask the parties. We need 10 minutes for the next witness to prepare. So we would then have one hour and 45 minutes. If we say we don't even start, fine, but I'd like to ask the parties after we finish this witness to see whether it's of any use to start, because it would mean approximately that for examination-in-chief it would be just a little bit over one hour, and for cross-examination approximately 40 minutes. I do not exclude, in view of earlier discussions between the parties specifically on this municipality, that it could be done, but -- so Mr. Stewart, we know that we are at a point that we really have to consider whether it's -- how to use our time. Please proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll use it for one question, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, it's in fact the case that when you went to hospital with your wound, you remained in the hospital for several days, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were visited by at least a couple of people that you knew from your own locality?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how long were you in hospital then?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about an hour. I was then taken to the Kljuc MUP or police station, and then I was taken to Bosanska Gradiska in a trailer with other prominent citizens of Kljuc. And around midnight we were placed in the prison in Gradska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I hope my questions didn't confuse. When I asked, "And you were visited by at least a couple of people that you knew from your own locality," you said yes. Perhaps I should make it clear: You were visited at the hospital by at least a couple of people that you knew from your own locality, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was visited by a number of persons because everyone in the hospital knew me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your evidence that in the course of one hour at the hospital, you received visits by a number of persons?

utterances.speaker: ASIM EGRLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Egrlic, I would like to thank you for having come to The Hague and for having answered the questions of both parties and the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to invite the parties, if it takes us 10 minutes to prepare this courtroom for the face and voice distortion, it has been prepared already but it has to be put in place now, then we would have, at the most, approximately 1 hour and 45, 50 minutes. That would mean 1 hour and 10 minutes for the Prosecution and 40 minutes for the Defence if we would finish by today. The parties may be aware that it's always -- it's not a preferred situation that you have to send a witness who has been waiting for quite some time here. I would like to invite the parties whether they think they could examine the witness in this time, and then we'll give it a try. But it needs the utmost discipline. It also needs the utmost discipline of the Chamber. Therefore, we'll immediately now have a break of 10 minutes so that the preparations can be made. --- Break taken at 11.57 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed that the parties thought they could finish the examination of the next witness, so it makes sense to start.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I was just indicating that I might ask to be excused at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you're going to take this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the witness could be escorted into the courtroom as soon as the curtains are down. Yes, you could already, Madam Usher. The next witness is a witness who will testify under pseudonym 188, face and voice distortion will be effective. Yes, thank you. Yes, Madam Usher, you've heard his feet are not to be hidden from the public, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 188, because that's how we're going to call you, before giving evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Could I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Your face will not be shown on the screen for the outside world. Your voice will be distorted so that you could not be recognised by your voice. And we'll call you Witness 188 in order to avoid the public to know your name and your identity. Mr. Resch, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could the witness first be shown the pseudonym sheet, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Resch:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you please look at the document in front of you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and confirm that that has your correct name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes, everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would have number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly cover some background information, sir, so if you could just listen to some of these questions and confirm that all the information I've stated is accurate. You were born and raised in the Biljani village in Kljuc Municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, you lived in Biljani with your mother, your father, and your grandmother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Resch, would you put out your microphone as soon as the witness answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your family was your mother and father, and they had eight children; five boys and three girls?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could now look at the map of the Biljani area, please. I believe it will show up on the Sanction monitor for the outside world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it would be P254. Mr. Resch, I take it that you'll be cautious not to indicate to anyplace that could reveal the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on this map, we see a small portion of Kljuc Municipality containing the Biljani village and some of the surrounding smaller hamlets. Is it correct that in 1992, the Biljani area contained approximately 2.000 inhabitants, and of those 80 per cent were Muslim, the other 20 per cent or so of the Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the neighbouring village area of Sanica in 1992 contained approximately 8.000 inhabitants, again with the roughly similar break-down of 80 per cent Muslim, 20 per cent Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes, 25/75, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in early 1992, did you notice a change in the atmosphere among the different ethnic groups in the Biljani and Sanica area of the Kljuc Municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In early 1992. In 1991 as well, but the results were more evident in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain, please, what this change in atmosphere was like.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Well, as I said, in 1991 towards the end of the year and in 1992, in view of the fact that I was engaged in my own private business, when I went out in the evening in Sanica, I noticed that people of one nationality went to one cafe and people of the other nationality went to another cafe. I happened to enter a cafe where ethnic Serbs gathered and the owner was a Muslim. I didn't know this. I went into the cafe with a friend. I ordered a drink. I was approached by a Serb who said, "What are you doing here?" And I said, "Well, I've come to have a drink." And he said, "This is no place for you. Go to the other cafe or you'll have problems." I just looked at the waiter. I drank some of my drink, and then I went out. And I said, "What's going on?" And the waiter said, "Well, people are dividing into Serbs and Muslims now."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately what time period did this event at the bar take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly when, but I do know it was winter, so it might have been in January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in 1992, were there checkpoints that went up in and around the Biljani and Sanica area, and accordingly restrictions on the movement of the population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Checkpoints were set up in March 1992, I think. And the checkpoints, well, it was only on the 25th of May, actually, that the checkpoints were set up between Sanica and Biljani at the bridge. A checkpoint was established at the bridge, and at the exit of Biljani in the area of Velagici so that movement was already restricted in the directions of Kljuc and Sanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which personnel of which ethnic background the people manning these checkpoints were? And specifically, the checkpoints on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: On the 25th of May, it was the reserve police force. Up to the 25th of May, there were Muslims employed in the police, but on the 25th of May, they disarmed the Muslims and sent them home and only policemen of Serb ethnicity were left there. And a checkpoint was set up. On that day, they were sent back from work. There was a sawmill in Sanica where my brother was employed and also my sister-in-law, and they were sent back home from work. They were told that they had no business in Sanica any more, that they should go home and wait to see what would happen to them next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware during 1991 and the early part of 1992 of efforts to provide arms, weapons, to the Serb population in Kljuc Municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Well, around the middle of 1991, there was a cafe in the Bravsko settlement on the Kljuc/Petrovic Road where I was working, and working on that cafe, one day, 25 to 30 men came. They said they were volunteers. They were armed. And they were getting ready to go to the war in Croatia. As I was working at the cafe, the owner said, "Finish your work. There's wood, and go and set up some targets for them for target practice." So that I observed in 1991 that they volunteered to go to the war theatre in Croatia and they voluntarily took up weapons, and as it happened, I constructed the targets for them to practice on. And in 1992 in March, I think it was early spring, as soon as the checkpoints were set up -- well no, I don't mean checkpoints, I mean observation posts and some sort of guards. On two occasions in April or March, I'm not sure exactly whether it was April or May, on two occasions I saw helicopters landing in the Gologlava area and also from time to time in Sanica. And in Sanica I heard from some relatives of mine that they came here and distributed weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be clear, you saw this helicopter land, but you only heard that there had been weapons distributed from the helicopter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next topic I'd like to cover is efforts to disarm the civilian population in Kljuc. In late May 1992, do you recall anyone coming into the village of Biljani and calling for weapons to be turned in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was on the 27th of May when the police station in Sanica was taken over. This was between the 25th and 27th of May. And they arrived that day in a van, and they had a loudspeaker on the van through which they announced that the Muslim people should hand in their weapons and take them to the railway station in Sanica. And this was done. And then again, I think on the 28th of May, there was someone who hadn't handed in his hunting weapon, and they came to the village with the van. It was Bosko Maric and Redzo Ajkic who came. One of them was a representative of the Muslims from Sanica, and they demanded that weapons be handed in and if this was not done the village would be shelled and someone would be killed. And the weapon was handed over, all the weapons were then handed over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned two names. Do you know which, if any, political party Bosko Maric was a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes, I think he belonged to the SDS party, and Redzo Ajkic was a representative of the SDA political party. At least, that's what I know because Maric for a time was a teacher in the primary school, and I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever join a political party in 1992 or before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, were you familiar with the SDS political leaders in Kljuc, the municipal level political leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: I didn't know them well at the municipal level because for the most part I looked to my business, to my work, and I was 13 kilometres away from Kljuc. So I'm not all that familiar with Kljuc. I just know what I heard. But I didn't know anyone personally, so I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd next like to ask you about the 30th of May. On that date, do you recall some soldiers coming to the Biljani village area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. On the 30th of May in the morning, it might have been 9.00 or 10.00, and I was about a hundred metres away from the main road, I could hear a large vehicle arriving. And when I looked there, I saw two APCs. They were olive grey. They were military vehicles. And there were 30 or 50 soldiers accompanying them. In front of the APCs, I noticed 20 or 30 men. And when they arrived at the entrance to the village, they stopped, and they sent these men into the village to tell us to go out on the main road. We were ordered to give a sign of loyalty or surrender, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond and this consisted in hanging out white sheets from the houses. And all adults between 18 and 60 were to go out onto the crossroads, and this was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's break that up into a few small parts. The -- by "APC," do you mean a military armoured personnel carrier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is a military armoured vehicle. There were two such vehicles, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers who were accompanying this APC, could you recognise any of these soldiers or were they -- were there any insignias or patches they were wearing which identified them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. All the soldiers, on their right shoulder, I think, had a piece of cloth of a certain colour. It was like a bow tied on one shoulder. And then on the sleeves, they had epaulets. And it said "The Army of Republika Srpska," I think, and some had White Eagle insignia or something like that. And many of them also had insignia on their caps, saying "SDS" and insignia of the white-headed eagle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there were 20 or 30 men walking in front of the APCs. Were these -- who were these men and where were they from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: These men came from the hamlet of Cehici, and when we arrived at the crossroads with them, they told those men that they could go home. And then they said, "Half of the men in your hamlet can go home, the elderly ones, and the rest of you will walk in front of us, and we will go in the direction of Jabukovac Polje, and don't let anything happen, don't let anyone shoot, because if there are any problems these men going in front will be killed first and they will be able to return home when we arrive at the villages of Jabukovac and Polje." When we arrived at the hamlet of Jabukovac, we were ordered to enter the village, and the soldiers stayed there, and we were ordered to go and tell the people to hang out white sheets and that all the men aged 18 to 60 should come out. When we did this, we were told that we could go home, and we did. When we got home, I learned from my mother, and I saw in my house, that when people came to the crossroads, the soldiers from the APCs entered the village and searched the houses looking for weapons. And they didn't find any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to recap, the 20 or 30 men that were forced to walk in front of the APCs as human shields were Muslims, and they were guarded or escorted by Serb soldiers from one village to the next in the process of searching these villages, these Muslim villages for weapons. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period of late May, say from the 25th of May through until June, was the -- your freedom of movement, was that restricted in the Sanica and Biljani area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was restricted by the checkpoint in Sanica, so we weren't able to get to Kljuc or go to Sanica (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: say that was up to May. It was the second or third day in May. And I couldn't go to the road. I couldn't get to the road for a number of months from my hamlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an occasion in early June when you tried to ride a bike to the hamlet of Jabukovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: That's correct. It's something I have already mentioned. I went to see how my sister was. And on my way to the hamlet, I thought that I would get there by bike very quickly since on the whole the road was used by vehicles travelling from Sanica. But these were Serbian vehicles, and at one point when I was returning from my sister's and as I was leaving Jabukovac, as I arrived, as I'd got to the road, I saw a lorry coming from the direction of Sanica. They opened fire from the lorry. I was afraid, and I hurried to hide behind the house. I managed to hide with my bicycle behind the house. I even fell off the bike. And then I noted they were shooting from behind since there were army reservists behind. They were probably coming from the battlefield because as they were passing down the road, they were going to the battlefields in Jajce or in Bihac, and they would then often open fire on the houses along the main road, so that they also opened fire on me. And once I had calmed down a bit, I returned home. But that was the last time I went to the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion when these soldiers fired at you, were you wearing a military uniform or carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, I was wearing a training suit and a T-shirt. Those are the clothes I would wear every day since it was summertime and I was on my bike, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In late June 1992, around the 27th, do you recall an occasion when some soldiers came to your village from Palanka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. This was again in the early morning hours. They came. We didn't know about what was happening. We didn't go out at all. One morning, they came from the upper part of the village -- young men came from the upper part of the village and said there were soldiers by the lake. They said they have surrounded the entire village, you can have a look. And in fact, when I had a look, about 70 or 80 metres from the house I could see there were soldiers. We were told to go to the lake, which is what we did. (redacted) (redacted) Everyone between 18 and 60 or 65 years of age went out, whereas the women and children remained at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Resch, would you please instruct the witness not to mention the name of what seems to be a very small hamlet where he lived because no redactions were made until now, and I would rather prevent that others should be made as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I think you understood the Presiding Judge's instruction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers that arrived on the 27th of June, were they led by an officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. There was an officer. He even introduced himself. And he said that they had come from Palanka, that they had been ordered to come there. He said that they had a certain list of people, and that these people would be questioned. And he also said that the houses would be searched. He said that whoever was innocent and whoever wasn't on the list would come to no harm and would return safely home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just turn briefly into private session for a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's confirmed on my screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers on this occasion, could you identify them, again by their uniforms or any insignia, as to where they were, what unit or army they were members of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: The commander introduced himself and said they had come from Palanka. They were wearing the uniforms of the then Yugoslav People's Army. On the whole, they had SDS insignia on them, and like their predecessors, they had these bands on their right shoulder of the same colour, and some individuals had the white-headed eagle sign and the SDS sign on their caps, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that were taken away that day, were they eventually returned to the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes, they were returned, and it was only in the evening hours that this happened since the person who was responsible to take them with him - this is what my brother told me - when they were supposed to return in two buses, this person asked what he should do with these people. The commander then said, "Take them behind the house, get rid of them. I'm not interested in it." And this person said, "Well, I can't do that. The people are innocent. We searched the houses and didn't find any weapons." He said, "If you don't want to do that, take them home with you." And he then put them in the bus, and several hundred metres later, when they stopped, he asked the commander again. And they said, okay, well let them go home if they're innocent. So the three of them were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, sir, I'd like to ask you about some events -- the events of the 10th of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: For Your Honours' information, this refers to Schedule A, incident 9.3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on the 10th of July, do you recall, starting from the earliest part of that day, at what time you woke up and what was happening when you woke up in your village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember what happened on the 10th of July. Very early in the morning, at 6.00, I heard the sound of shooting, and I realised that something was wrong. And when I went out of the house, a few of us gathered and we thought we would be doing some sort of work. But 15 minutes later, from the upper part of the town, the young men arrived and said that we should all gather at the place called Jezerina. Everyone between 18 and 60 years of age should gather. And the order was that only women and children should remain at home. And this is what happened. I was dressed in my training suit and T-shirt, and my father remained at home. And that's how I set off. I set off with my brother and the others. We went to a field in front of the village itself. And when I had a look around at the village, I noticed 20 or 30 soldiers on each elevation. So the village was completely surrounded and cut off. So when we got to Jezerina, they lined us up. Marko Samardzija was waiting for us there. He was there with Mladjo Tesic and about another ten soldiers. They were all neighbours. They said, "Don't be afraid. Nothing will happen to you. We have come here. We have a list with us. Whoever is not -- whoever is on the list will be questioned and taken away. If people aren't on the list, they will be sent back." As they knew -- as we knew that we didn't have any weapons and we weren't on a list of any kind, I was hoping that we would be sent back home, as they had promised. We remained there for about one hour. Once they had lined us up and approached us -- well, in the meantime they searched the village to make sure that no one had remained there. And then they used the radio, and we were told that we should go to the primary school in Biljani. We went there two by two in a column. And we went as far as the centre in Biljani. On the way there, since the school is about a kilometre away, it was possible to notice that there were quite a lot of soldiers from the Republika Srpska. There were quite a lot of reservists. And when we arrived at the school, there were two trees in front of the school, and there was a van under the first tree, and about ten special policemen. They had these white belts on them. And under the other tree, there was the police commander Tomic. I knew him myself, I knew him personally. Mihic was there, and the director of a certain factory was there, I can't remember his name, and there were several other persons. Marko Samardzija approached, greeted them, shook hands. We were then told to enter the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I stop you there and ask first, you mentioned Marko Samardzija. Do you know if Marko Samardzija was an officer? And if so, what rank he held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Marko Samardzija was part of the reserve forces. And he was a captain. I know him personally because he was my teacher in primary school in Biljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a police commander, Mile Tomic. From where was Mile Tomic a commander, a police commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: I know he's from Kljuc since he's not from Sanica, but he was the police commander in Sanica. But I don't really know which village he is from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many Muslim men from your village, from your hamlet, were taken prisoner and marched to the elementary school in Biljani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: About 60 people from our hamlet. We were all taken into one classroom. We had previously been searched. We had to empty our pockets and leave everything and leave our documents in the corridor and enter the classroom in this state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mile Tomic, this police commander from Sanica. Were there any other police officers accompanying Tomic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Since Tomic was under the other tree, well, there was Mihic there, his deputy. I also know him personally because he worked as a television repairman. And under the other tree, there were special policemen from Kljuc. They weren't together. They were about 5 or 7 metres away from the other group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the police, how many soldiers were guarding or escorting you and the other men from your hamlet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: There were between 50 to 70 people from our hamlet. So from my hamlet, when we arrived in front of the school, there were hundreds of soldiers around the school. There were about 10 soldiers in front of the shop where they had already brought women and children from another hamlet. They were guarding them there. And as I said, they were arriving from all directions. Since our village consists of seven to eight hamlets, these soldiers came from each of the hamlets and they brought people with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the one-page -- the first exhibit, the one-page police document from the 10th of July 1992 and that be given an exhibit number. I believe it will also show up on the monitors; the English on Sanction, and perhaps we could put the original on the ELMO for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it's even better to put the original to the witness right away so that he can better read it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The number would be, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number will be P255 and P255.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an official note dated 10 July 1992, signed at the bottom by the commander of the Sanica SRM.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to read to you the second full paragraph in the document, which reads: "On the evening of 9 July 1992, I was informed by the commander of the battalion quartered in Sanica that on 10 July his units would undertake a mopping-up operation of the terrain, meaning the area of the villages Gornji Biljani and Donji Biljani. Therefore, it was necessary that the police workers of the SRM join in the action as well." Sir, is that consistent that police officers were in Biljani, is that consistent with what you saw on the 10th of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. When we entered the classroom, the deputy commander of the police, Mihic Petar, came together with his colleague Lazo, who was also from Biljani. Since they were in the Sanica police station, it was their duty in our classroom where there were over a hundred of us, it was their duty to write down our names and include them in a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Could we now have the next short document shown to the witness - this is also -- this is actually a document dated 9 July 1992 - and given an exhibit number. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be P256 for the original in B/C/S and P256.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the document in front of you is an order dated 9 July 1992 from Kljuc military post 2207, signed by Commander Lieutenant Colonel I believe it's Drago Samardzija. It's easier to read on the original. On the first page, under item 1, it states: "Readiness for operation 0500 hours on 10 July 1992." Is that consistent -- let me actually read what's under item number 2 as well. Under 2 (a), assignments for units, the document reads: "The 2nd Battalion of the 17th Light Infantry Brigade, reinforced with a reconnaissance platoon, a military police squad, and a police platoon is to block, search, and mop-up the Donji Biljani, Domazeti, Botonjici, Jabukovac, Osmanovici, and Brkici sectors." Is that information consistent with what you saw in your hamlet and eventually at the school in Biljani on the 10th of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. This is what happened. That's correct, since the inhabitants of Gologlava and the Loncari hamlets brought us in, and from the direction of Sanica there was the reserve force there involved in mopping-up Jabukovac Polje. And from the Botonjici hamlet, there was another company involved there, engaged there. And then there was the hamlet of Kolici [phoen] and Pistanica and Domazeti, and it was probably their task to deal with the Samardzija hamlet and Osljak and so on. So I fully agree with this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if there was any relationship between Drago Samardzija, who signed this order, and Marko Samardzija, the captain you saw on the 10th of July 1992? Any family relationship?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Since I didn't know Drago Samardzija, and I don't think he's from the Biljani area since Marko Samardzija was born in Biljani and he was a teacher of mine. But I don't know Drago Samardzija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before I showed you the documents, you mentioned when all the prisoners were brought to the school, you were placed inside and the police commander Mihic came in, told everyone to calm down and started making a list. At some point, did someone return with the list and call people's names out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. It took about 45 minutes to make the list, and once it had been done, they said that everything would be dealt with quickly, that they just wanted to check the list. And then after 10 or 15 minutes, he returned with the list and read out the names of ten persons from the list. He only said that he wanted to check whether they were there. I think that of the ten of them whose names he read out, nine of them were in my classroom, and they all said that they were present. He then left and didn't come back for 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he came back, did he ask these men whose names he had called to leave the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. He read out their names one by one. They didn't all leave at the same time. First they left one after another -- five minutes after each other, and then every few minutes you could hear a burst of fire. I remember very well that when one of them was leaving the classroom, a relative of mine, a policeman told him, when he said that he had forgotten his jacket, a policeman told him that he could leave it there because he wouldn't need it any more. And then after he had left, a few minutes later there was a burst of fire we could hear. The policeman who was guarding us in the classroom said, "Don't be afraid. It's the Green Berets who are attacking. We will calm them down and drive them away now. We will deal with that very quickly, there are quite a few of us here." When they had read out the names of these ten people, after they had left, there was another 5- to 10-minute break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that break, were you called out and asked to leave the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: No, they didn't read out any more names. Instead, they said that five by five men should stand in front of the door and go out. We should go out in groups of five. And when the next group of five went out, the same things happened as before. When the first five went out, the shooting outside intensified, as did the screams of men. At one point, because I was sitting next to the window on a bench, I looked out. When we were coming to the school, we saw two buses parked near the school. When we looked out, we saw that people were passing through the line and were being beaten, and some were falling down. And I also saw some people being taken away to the road below. And then when some 20 or 30 men had left the classroom, panic arose in the classroom because one of the men there said, "They're going to kill us all. Let's hurry up and get on the buses." I was near the door then of the schoolroom, and then confusion ensued. A soldier came in and told us to calm down. He said we would all be going. Before this, in fact, before he said we would all be going, he said that the elderly men should go to one side of the classroom because only the younger men would be travelling. It was our turn next, and we went out into the corridor. In the corridor, they stopped us again, and they started letting us out one by one. I was the last in that group of five. And when the third man went out, I was able to see outside and I saw some 20 or 30 soldiers lined up, and there was another soldier standing on the steps. And when this man started going down, they would follow him and beat him. At the door, he asked me very briefly, "Where are your weapons? What have you done here?" And things like that. And then he told me to get out. When I got out, the man before me who had been standing on the steps went with a neighbour beating him and saying, "You thought you'd escape me." This neighbour was a well-known person, and he beat him until he got onto the bus. And that's how I managed to get down the steps without being beaten. Dragan Cvijic was standing at the bottom of the steps. I knew him personally. He was a special-purpose policeman. I recognised him as soon as we arrived at the school. I knew him because I used to work in cafes, and he worked in one of the cafes where I worked. And as he had a good look at me and turned away, I thought, well, finally he recognised me and now he'll save me. As I was passing by him, he just turned to me and kicked me in the stomach. And then he punched me. This was when I realised I had to hurry and get on the bus, so I passed quickly by the next ten men in order to get onto the bus as soon as possible. As I was entering the bus, a soldier bent me over his leg because there were several steps, and he said to me, "Do you want to sit down?" I didn't know what to reply because whatever I said I knew it would be the wrong answer. And then I felt them hitting me with batons, with sticks, and with chains. When the next men arrived, he let me get on the bus. He pushed me so that I went all the way to the back door because all the seats were already full. He pushed me all the way back and made me sit on the floor next the back door of the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were packed into this school bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: At that point -- there were about 50 seats in the bus. At that point, there weren't more than 50. I was the second or third person who had to sit on the floor near the back door. This went on for another 15 or 20 minutes, not longer, until that bus was packed. All the time I was on the bus, I heard people being beaten as they were brought to the bus. And if one of them fell down, they would say, "Take him away. This man is good for nothing. Kill him." I remember very well when another man came along who worked in the Kljuc Municipality, and he said, "Give this one to me. This one is not getting on the bus." And then when the bus was already full, there was a pause, and then they said, "What shall we do with the rest of them?" And one of the chief men was sitting near the tree, and he said, "We don't need the rest of them. Kill them all. One bus is enough." And then you could hear chaos. The bursts of fire didn't stop. Whenever somebody fell or was beaten, they would all yell with pleasure. And when they said the bus could go to Kljuc, the driver complained that his tyres had been deflated. He drove for about 10 metres, and he stopped when we got onto the asphalt road. And he said, "I can't go to Kljuc like this. The bus is too heavy." A soldier came in and said, "Give me four men. I'll rid you of four of them." At that point, he was choosing four strong men, so I thought he needed them to do a loading job or something or to move corpses. He selected a relative of mine and three other men and took them away. The bus stood there for only a few minutes, not longer, and then set out again. But 50 metres on, it stopped between two houses and they said, "You will now be moved onto another bus." Three or four soldiers, or rather special-purpose military policemen with white belts wearing camouflage uniforms, came in and said, "I don't want the men in front. Give me five from the back." I was near the door, and there were other neighbours sitting near where I was sitting, and we moved toward the other bus. The other bus was only five metres away. I was already running towards the bus, hoping to find a seat inside. However, as I was boarding the bus, there were five or six soldiers with white belts already inside. They said, "No, this is no place for you, you go in through the back door." So I was the last in line when I got to the back door of the bus. And as soon as we got to the back of the bus, I realised we weren't being taken to that bus, that we would probably be killed. They took us a few metres, near a house, and the first man in the line stopped and said, "What's this?" I was standing behind the man in front of me. I had my hands on my head, and there was a gun in my back. And when I had to cross a small ditch, I saw my relative lying in the ditch, and three other men. They had been killed. At that moment, I knew -- I was sure we would be killed. The first man probably started running off to the right. My neighbour and I started running off to the left. A second or two later, we heard them yelling, "Stop." They called us balijas. And then we heard a burst of fire. I didn't feel anything. I just saw my neighbour falling down in front of me with two or three huge holes in his back. And quite mechanically, not even knowing what was going on, completely unconsciously, I fell to the ground next to him. I heard them changing their clips, and there was another burst of fire. And I had a little time to think while they were changing their clips. And I thought, well, if they wound me, I'll clench my teeth because I had heard previously that in Velagici, a few men survived the execution. They were wounded, and they survived the execution. So I thought if this happens to me, I'll try. However, I remained not wounded even during the second burst of fire. I was very close to my relative, and I was wearing a purple T-shirt, and I was probably stained with his blood. They stopped for a while, and I heard them looking to see if we were alive. Somebody yelled, "The one to the right in the multicoloured T-shirt, he's still alive. Finish him off." And then this other one fired another burst of fire at the man in the multicoloured T-shirt. And then you could hear from the bus people yelling, "Hurry up, you down there, we're off to Kljuc." And they fired a fourth burst of fire. They were waiting for us to stop breathing. When they killed this man Rufad, and when I heard this burst of fire, I sensed them running back to the bus. The engines of the buses were switched on and they set off towards Kljuc. You could hear bursts of fire throughout the whole village. I didn't know what was going on. I remained lying there quite still. And some 10 minutes later you could hear soldiers all around. There was a cafe in that house, and a certain number of people were there in front of the cafe. And I could hear their conversations. I heard everything they were saying. I was still lying there quite still without moving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I stop you there for a moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: And ask, Your Honour, that we turn to private session for the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: With the leave of the Court, I would just like to be fairly direct with a final few questions to finish off the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, have you any idea how much time you would need for cross-examination? Because as I said, we have no margins. Mr. Stewart, how much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think it's going to be a problem this afternoon, Your Honour. I assume that these few questions where Mr. Resch is going to lead the witness, he's talking about relatively harmless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Mr. Resch finishes in the next five minutes, we'll finish within the normal time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then, please...

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Agreed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 10th of July at Biljani, was Fikret Balagic one of the men called out from the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: No, no, his name wasn't called out. He left the classroom together with me and we went to the bus together. Or rather, he was in front of me in the line-up for execution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Hamdija Domazet? Was he there on the 10th of July also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the events of the 10th of July, is it correct that you made it to Kljuc town and managed to hide either in the town or in and around that town until sometime in September 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: First, I hid in my hamlet until September. And in September, I moved to Kljuc, and I think on the 10th of September this was. And on the 19th or 20th of September, I went to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went to Travnik in a convoy that went over -- passed Skender Vakuf, over Mount Vlasic, and eventually you made it to Travnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the time you left the Biljani area in 1992, of the approximately 1600 Muslim inhabitants, how many remained in the Biljani area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: When I left, about half remained. At the end of September, the remaining half left out. And after September, I think only 10 or 15 inhabitants were left in Biljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that approximately the same number of Muslim inhabitants who remained in the Sanica village area by late September 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. About 10 more, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's the end of my examination. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Resch. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Stewart, who is counsel for the Defence. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in your evidence today, you referred to some men who had what you described as SDS insignia on their clothing. Well, first of all, is that what you meant to say, an SDS insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Well, on their sleeves, they had four Ss, the letter S appeared four times. There is the cross and the letter S which occurs four times. I apologise, perhaps I said the SDS, but the sign I had in mind was the sign of the four Ss. I think that that is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would accept, would you, that that's not an SDS insignia at all.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Yes. For me, they are only Serbs. Every soldier had those signs. Many of them had the Ss, and they had the white-headed eagle on them. But a lot of time has passed, so each soldier had a badge on the left sleeve, and the letter S appeared four times on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave an answer which is a few lines on the transcript. Your answer started with "Yes" in answer to my question, "You would accept, would you, that that's not an SDS insignia at all." Can I take it that the answer to my question is yes, you would accept that that's not an SDS insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: Well, it's the same thing for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the same thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to cut it short. You described insignia, four Ss on it. Has this insignia got anything to do specifically with the SDS being a political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Because when I said that there were four Ss, well, it's not really the same thing. But at that time, I said the SDS because I had forgotten about the four Ss. But I was thinking of the four Ss because that was the sign that appeared on their sleeves. I apologise if I expressed myself incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing Mr. Stewart does at this moment is to seek confirmation that the four Ss insignia are not linked specifically to the political party SDS. That, as far as I understand you, is a more general --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But many of the them had SDS insignia on them, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll give it over to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That takes us back to the beginning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm inviting you -- it's an invitation; you're giving evidence, Witness. I'm inviting you to confirm that whatever insignia you saw with those Ss had nothing with the SDS as a political party.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This started with your evidence that it was SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Resch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll stipulate that there was no link between the four Ss and the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's not part of the Prosecutor's case that there was an SDS insignia on the shoulders apart from the four Ss.

utterances.speaker: MR. RESCH
utterances.text: That's the Prosecution case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do love a good stipulation, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Resch. Witness, could you be shown, please, Exhibit P251.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you find, please -- I seem to remember from some time ago it's on page 8 of the document, you've got a heading, it's number VI, "The course of armed operations." Can you find that heading. It's a VI, then "The course of armed operations." Let His Honour know when you've found that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Crljeni, as I think it is, is how far from -- roughly within 5 kilometres will do, from where you live?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel repeat the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll have one go, and then I'll ask Ms. Cmeric. Crljeni, C-R-L-J-E-N-I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at a distance of 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at item 6 under that heading VI, "Capture of seven Serbian BH soldiers." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's only about three or four lines. So if you could just read that item and then tell the Trial Chamber whether you know anything at all about that incident as reported there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: As I said, Crljeni was 20 kilometres from Kljuc. I only heard about this later on, when I went to Travnik. But initially, I didn't hear about the incident in Crljeni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what you've heard now, or heard since, rather, indicates that it did happen in the terms described there, does it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: I heard about it. And I know the soldiers were released and that nothing happened. I know that nothing, in fact, happened in Crljeni. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that what you have heard indicates that this didn't happen as described in this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: I wouldn't comment on that. I don't know anything about Crljeni.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. I'm going to have to press you to comment. I'm simply asking whether what you have heard indicates to you that this did happen as reported here or didn't happen as reported here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask you, draw your attention to the answer of the question which is, "I heard about it. And I know the soldiers were released and that nothing happened." That's how it appears in the transcript. "I know that nothing, in fact, in Crljeni happened." That's what I heard. Read in the context, I think the part of the answer which reads, "and that nothing happened" would need further clarification since it seems not to be a total denial of anything happening in Crljeni.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I acknowledge we've got a slightly untidy position as far as the evidence so far is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take it in little bits. It won't take long, Witness. What you have heard indicates that, yes, on the 25th of May 1992, seven soldiers were captured in that village. Is that right? That you have heard that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear that they were deployed on reconnoitering the terrain in a unit on Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about that. I said I was about 20 kilometres away and I didn't receive any kind of information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to save time. We won't worry about item 1. But there are four fairly short items above item 6 there, 2, 3, 4, and 5. Would you just read those and say whether you know anything about those incidents from anything you knew at the time, what you've since heard, whether you know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: As I said, we were 13 kilometres from Kljuc in Biljani, and from this place about 12 kilometres away. The first week we didn't hear anything, but we did receive information and I'll tell you exactly what sort of information we received. We received information that some troops returned, that they were waited for in Busija, that these soldiers were recruits. We heard that there was an incident, and I know nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it you have been able quickly to read 2, 3, 4, and 5, or you haven't read them as I invited you to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: No, I haven't read them, but I know what I heard and I know what it relates to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without having read them, you can -- 2, 3, 4, and 5 -- maybe so, I'm just asking you to confirm; you've had a sufficient chance to look at 2, 3, 4, and 5 to know the four incidents that they are referring to, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 188
utterances.text: At the time I wasn't aware of four incidents, I was only aware of one incident. That's the only thing I had knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber prefers that the witness is in the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond ordinary way escorted out of the courtroom.
