utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber delivers its oral decision on the Defence motion for the translation of documents into B/C/S. This is the decision on the Defence motions of the 23rd of July 2004 calling upon the Chamber to order that all transcripts of proceedings in the present case be provided to the accused in hard-copy translation. The Defence also requests that the same be ordered in relation to all transcripts of prior proceedings of this Tribunal which are admitted into evidence pursuant to Rules 89(f) and 92 bis. The Defence proposes a different regime for four other categories of documents; namely, Rule 92 bis documents in general, Rule 94 bis (c) statements, Rule 66(b) material, and Rule 68 material. Concerning documents in these categories, the Defence proposes to certify on a case-by-case basis that a translation of a certain document is necessary for the proper conduct of the accused's Defence. If the Prosecution were to disagree with this assessment of the Defence, the matter would be brought before the Trial Chamber for a ruling. The reasons behind the Defence motion and the arguments in support of it are explained in the written motion and need not to be repeated here. The Prosecution has indicated that it opposes the Defence motion, although mainly in view of the practical consequences rather than the fundamental opposition against it. As the situation stands now, the accused has access to B/C/S audio recordings of the present proceedings. He also has access, or at least should have access, so if he has not, the Chamber would like to be informed, to B/C/S audio recordings of any relevant past proceedings, and in particular, to B/C/S recordings corresponding to the transcripts of past proceedings admitted into evidence here pursuant to Rules 89(f) and 92 bis. The accused receives, as a rule, translations of non-B/C/S exhibits and expert reports in evidence. Other items are read into the record and thereby receive interpretation. The Defence team includes one or more members who speak the language of the accused. The question is whether the situation as it stands derogates from the accused's right to have adequate time and facilities to prepare his Defence in accordance with Article 21 of the Statute and the practice of this Tribunal. In 1996, the Delalic Trial Chamber stated as follows: "The Trial Chamber ... finds that all material accompanying the indictment that the Prosecution is required to make available for the Defence pursuant to Rule 66(a) must be in the language of the accused, irrespective of whether it will be offered at trial." And the Delalic Trial Chamber continued in paragraph 8: "The Trial Chamber finds that neither Rule 3 nor Article 21 entitles the Defence to receive all discovery from the Prosecution in the language of the accused. The guarantees of Article 21(4) do not extend to all material but only to evidence which forms the basis of the determination by the Trial Chamber of the charges against the accused. ... The rights of the accused are fully protected by ensuring that all evidence submitted at trial is provided in his language. The Trial Chamber finds that discovery provided by the parties to each other shall be in the original language of the document, if that is the language of the accused, or in one of the working languages of the International Tribunal. If the original language of the document is one other than the language of the accused or one of the working languages, discovery shall be in one of the working languages." Both quotes, one from paragraph 6 and the other from paragraph 8, there are a few irrelevant parts left out, so they are not complete quotes of the part I read. Thus, the Delalic Trial Chamber understood the right of the accused to receive documents beyond the supporting materials, so to receive documents in his own language, to be limited to those documents which are submitted at trial as evidence. This would immediately dispense with the Defence request that it be given the right to more or less decide which Rule 66(b) material and which Rule 68 material it should have translated at the Tribunal's expense. The Delalic Trial Chamber made this additional determination in paragraph 12: "During all of its proceedings the International Tribunal has interpreters whose responsibility it is to provide simultaneous interpretation of the proceedings into the language of the accused. This system satisfies the requirement of Article 21(4)(f) and ensures the right of the accused to understand the nature and cause of the charge against him under Article 21(4)(a)." The present Chamber is aware that this last quote did not directly address Article 21(4)(b), and in particular on the part adequate time and facilities. However, the Delalic assessment in the last quote does have a bearing on the present issue. This is because Delalic went on to find, and I now quote from paragraph 14: "As with motions and other similar documents [which do not fit within the parameters of the evidence upon which a Trial Chamber bases its determination of the charges against the accused] the Defence is not entitled to have transcripts translated into the language of the accused." And this requires a note of explanation. Transcripts of the present proceedings are a particular kind of record of the evidence presented in the course of the present proceedings. They are not themselves the evidence. The oral evidence is interpreted for the accused. Although the interpretation is not transcribed, it is, however, recorded. This B/C/S record, the audio recording, is available to the accused. So the position of the Trial Chamber in Delalic implies that an accused does have a right to have the evidence provided to him in his own language, but this right does not include a translation of the hard-copy record of the proceedings. In the Naletelic case, in a decision of the 18th of October 2001, the Trial Chamber followed the Delalic decision closely, saying: "The guarantees provided in Article 21(4) of the Statute do not extend to all documents but only to evidence which forms the basis of the determination by the Chamber of the charges against the accused; and ... this right is ensured, inter alia, by the fact that all evidence admitted at trial is provided in a language the accused understands." This entitlement was later -- at a later stage was narrowed further by an oral decision acknowledged by the Defence in the paragraphs 21 and 22 of its motion. In another case, the accused Zigic was exceptionally allowed to receive in a language which he understands all documents directly relating to his appeal, but that was because he was at that point without legal representation. Decision of the 3rd of October 2002. And the same pre-Appeal Judge emphasised in a later decision that he had not meant that Zigic would receive in translation at the Tribunal expense material that was only peripheral to his appeal. That decision was taken the 27th of November of that same year. Of Tribunal cases, the Chamber would finally mention one where, again for exceptional circumstances, an accused - I say "an accused" because it was a decision given in closed session - was allowed to receive I would say only some lines in translation at the Tribunal's expense. I now refer to the European Court cases cited by the Defence. Only the Luedicke case - that's Luedicke, Belkacem and Koc versus Germany - is at all relevant. The main question in that case was whether the defendants could be made to foot the bill for the interpretation costs of the proceedings, which of course not at this moment is an issue here. The Court said: "The right to a fair trial guaranteed by Article 6 paragraph 3(e) signifies that an accused who cannot understand or speak the language used in court has the right to the free assistance of an interpreter for the translation or interpretation of all those documents or statements in the proceedings instituted against him which it is necessary for him to understand in order to have the benefit of a fair trial." This is not different from the position taken by the Delalic Trial Chamber. The Kamasinski case before the European Court of Human Rights, dealing extensively with matters of interpretation and translation, also does not support the Defence position. It follows from the above that an accused does not have a general right to the translation of documents in the categories indicated by the Defence, whether automatically or according to the self-regulating regime proposed by the Defence except insofar as the document in question is a proposed item of evidence which is admitted into evidence. The Chamber notes that transcripts of evidence of past proceedings have come to be treated as items of evidence in their own right. For example, Rule 92 bis transcripts are now assigned exhibit numbers. Nevertheless, as with transcripts of the present proceedings, the Chamber regards the transcripts of past proceedings as mere records of evidence not requiring translation because a corresponding B/C/S audio recording is available to the accused. The Defence has also not convinced the Chamber that the accused has any special right arising out of the particular features of this case. The Defence has not indicated any circumstances which the Chamber would consider exceptional. The Chamber is not convinced by the Defence submissions in paragraph 29 of the motion that the use of audio recordings is burdensome and oppressive for Mr. Krajisnik. The transcription of an audio recording would of course be easier to use, but that does not necessarily render all potential methods of working with the audio recording unacceptably inefficient. The Defence has certainly not shown that any inefficiency related to the use of audio recordings by the accused has compromised his right to a fair trial. Nothing I've said so far excludes the possibility that the Chamber will authorise translation of certain documents or certain classes of documents in exceptional circumstances. In conclusion, the Trial Chamber dismisses the motion in its entirety. That's the decision on the motion. Then I'd like to make two very brief remarks: The first one is that the Chamber is aware of ongoing negotiations between the Association of Defence Counsel and the Registry on the policy of issues of translation and interpretation. I take it since Ms. Loukas is on the board of the ADC that she is certainly aware of that. The second issue I'd just like to mention, and nothing more, is that, Mr. Krajisnik, the Chamber inquired into problems related to laptop computers used in court and the Detention Unit. It seems to be a rather complex matter, but we try to get full oversight of it and I'll then at a later stage come back to that. The tape is running out. I think from now on in one minute, if there's any very urgent issue that should be raised before the recess, I'd like to hear it now.

I will hear from the parties if that's necessary.
